stem: A nurse sustains a percutaneous exposure to blood from a patient with known hepatitis C virus infection. Which follow-up is appropriate?

options.A: Start direct-acting antiviral treatment after every HCV exposure before baseline testing because immediate prophylaxis is standard.
options.B: Obtain baseline and indicated follow-up HCV testing because occupational HCV postexposure prophylaxis is not routinely recommended.
options.C: Give hepatitis C immune globulin and omit follow-up testing if the needlestick site was washed promptly after exposure.
options.D: Give an HCV vaccine series and check post-vaccination immunity instead of arranging baseline and follow-up laboratory testing.

rationale: CDC recommends baseline HCP testing as soon as possible, preferably within 48 hours, using anti-HCV with reflex HCV RNA if positive. When follow-up is indicated because the source is HCV RNA positive, NAT for HCV RNA is recommended at 3–6 weeks and final anti-HCV testing at 4–6 months if the earlier NAT is negative. CDC does not routinely recommend HCV postexposure prophylaxis with direct-acting antivirals. Therefore B is correct.
educational_objective: After occupational HCV exposure, obtain prompt baseline and indicated follow-up testing rather than routine antiviral postexposure prophylaxis.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_document_title: Testing and Clinical Management of Health Care Personnel Potentially Exposed to Hepatitis C Virus — CDC Guidance, United States, 2020
source_version_date: CDC guidance July 24, 2020; current CDC HCP guidance page updated April 24, 2024 and live-rechecked August 16, 2026
source_locator: Test the HCP > Baseline Testing; HCV PEP Not Recommended; Testing 3–6 Weeks Postexposure; final anti-HCV testing 4–6 Months Postexposure. Current CDC HCP page repeats the same algorithm: baseline preferably within 48 hours, NAT at 3–6 weeks when indicated, final testing at 4–6 months, and no routine HCV PEP.
source_claim_supported: Occupational HCV exposure requires prompt baseline testing and indicated follow-up testing; routine HCV PEP with direct-acting antivirals is not recommended.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)

source_original.stem: A nurse sustains a percutaneous exposure to blood from a patient with known hepatitis C virus infection. Which follow-up is appropriate?

options.A: Start direct-acting antiviral treatment after every HCV exposure before baseline testing because immediate prophylaxis is standard.
options.B: Obtain baseline and indicated follow-up HCV testing because occupational HCV postexposure prophylaxis is not recommended.
options.C: Give hepatitis C immune globulin and omit follow-up testing if the needlestick site was washed promptly after the exposure.
options.D: Give an HCV vaccine series and check post-vaccination immunity rather than arranging baseline and follow-up laboratory testing.

source_original.rationale: CDC recommends baseline testing and indicated follow-up testing after occupational HCV exposure. HCV postexposure prophylaxis is not recommended, and no HCV vaccine is available.
source_original.source_detail: Test the HCP > Baseline Testing; HCV PEP Not Recommended; Testing 3–6 weeks after exposure; Testing 4–6 months after exposure. CDC Guidance, United States, 2020; current CDC occupational guidance applicability rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Overview of Content — Safety and Infection Prevention and Control, printed p.8: infection prevention, biohazard handling, security plans, equipment safety and workplace safety. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Retained the occupational-HCV construct and key B, tightened the PEP wording to 'not routinely recommended,' linked the original 2020 MMWR algorithm to the current 2024 CDC HCP page, and reduced difficulty from hard to medium.

audit_findings.source_authority: CDC MMWR occupational HCV guidance plus current CDC HCP page; NCSBN 2026 Test Plan
audit_findings.currentness: Current CDC HCP page updated 2024-04-24 and live-rechecked 2026-08-16; algorithm remains consistent with 2020 MMWR guidance
audit_findings.exact_locator: Baseline Testing; HCV PEP Not Recommended; 3–6 Weeks; 4–6 Months
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final item accurately distinguishes recommended testing from routine antiviral prophylaxis and preserves the conditional nature of follow-up testing.

distractor_audit.A: Incorrect because routine DAA PEP for all occupational HCV exposures is not recommended.
distractor_audit.C: Incorrect because washing does not replace indicated laboratory follow-up and HCV immune globulin is not the recommended strategy.
distractor_audit.D: Incorrect because the recommended occupational approach is laboratory testing, not a vaccination strategy.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only B matches the CDC occupational exposure algorithm.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are postexposure management strategies with similar structure.
audit_findings.blueprint: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — occupational exposure management.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Re-read the 2020 MMWR and current 2024 CDC HCP page, all options, timing windows, rationale and NCSBN mapping. B remained uniquely correct.
